title: Texas payrolls enter year-end near a standstill after benchmark revisions
summary: The Dallas Fed's 9 January estimate put Texas payroll growth close to zero over 2025. Its central projection implied a loss of 2,200 jobs from December to December and a December employment level of roughly 14.2 million. The 80% confidence band for full-year growth extended from −0.3% to +0.3%. The sign of the small annual change was therefore uncertain. The stronger message was the departure from the 2% long-term average growth rate cited by Dallas Fed economist Luis Torres. The forecast was published after the end of 2025 but before the December payroll observation was available. Its projection of 0.5% annualised growth in December should be read as a forecast of a single month's pace.

The weakness reflected two developments with different economic meanings. Recent payrolls fell in October and November, by 5,600 and 4,600 jobs respectively. Those were annualised monthly declines of 0.5% and 0.4%. The loss over the three months ending in November was larger, at approximately 23,000 jobs. In addition, benchmark revisions reduced employment growth between March and June by 2.6 percentage points. That revision changed the measured starting point for assessing the latter part of the year. It did not represent a fresh round of layoffs in November. Together with weak late-year hiring, the earlier revisions left the reported 2025 growth rate through November at −0.1%. This is a different interval from the full-year estimate and from the annualised monthly rates.

The weakness was uneven across industries and cities. Torres identified professional and business services and oil and gas as the largest sources of November losses, with federal government employment also contributing to the decline in both October and November. Austin continued to add jobs at a solid pace while other major Texas metropolitan areas were flat or down. He offered two possible mechanisms for subdued hiring: rising productivity reduced the labour required for production, while lower immigration constrained the available workforce. The release does not estimate the relative contribution of these explanations. The interpretation is consequential because a fall in employment driven by weaker output differs from one driven by tighter labour supply or greater output per worker.

The Texas Leading Index weakened slightly in the three months through November. Chart 2 puts its net change at −0.49%, with new unemployment claims subtracting the most among the components shown. Oil prices, the US leading index, well permits and the Texas value of the dollar also weighed on the index. State equity prices, help-wanted activity and the average workweek contributed positively. Those offsetting components are a reason to avoid reading the negative headline as a uniformly weak signal. Chart 1 uses two axes: seasonally adjusted jobs are shown in millions on the left and the leading index is based at 100 in 1987 on the right. Their movements can be compared through time, but the distance between the lines has no interpretation as an employment shortfall.

The annual estimate averages four models. Three vector autoregressions use lagged information from oil prices and state or national leading indicators. The fourth also uses payroll history, US GDP growth and West Texas Intermediate prices, with US GDP forecasts and oil futures supplying forward inputs. The methodology includes adjustments for the pandemic period. Neither those forecasts nor prices of oil futures are direct observations of future Texas employment. The note supplies a state-level labour baseline and an uncertainty band, rather than evidence for a particular change in US policy rates. An investor using the estimate to assess Texas-exposed revenues or credit quality would need to establish which of the observed sectoral changes reach household incomes, borrower cash flows or demand for local services.

questions.question: How much of the deterioration was visible in real time?
questions.detail: The benchmark revision lowered first-half growth substantially, while the late-year payroll declines were separate observations. For an investor evaluating the timeliness of a state labour signal, compare the archived Dallas Fed forecast vintages and benchmarked payroll releases at identical observation dates. This would distinguish a genuine turning point from a retrospective change in the path.

questions.question: Did productivity, labour supply or weaker demand dominate?
questions.detail: Torres identifies productivity and immigration, while the leading index also shows weakness in claims and energy-sensitive indicators. The release does not quantify these channels. Examine sectoral output and hours, employment and participation, earnings and vacancies in the affected metros. Different combinations would imply different pressures on firms' revenues and wage bills even with identical statewide payroll growth.

questions.question: Which forecast inputs could move the result beyond its uncertainty band?
questions.detail: Oil prices, national activity and state indicators all enter the model set, but the article provides no sensitivities for a given oil or GDP surprise. Consult the Dallas Fed methodology and component forecasts, then compare revisions across subsequent forecast vintages. An energy-sensitive credit or regional demand view needs to know whether a change in one input drives a broad revision or is offset by other components.
